issues.title: Overall scope - what forms of IETF-related text are in/out of scope?
issues.author: sftcd
issues.body:
Issue raised in discussion of #1 

What IETF communications should be in scope for the draft?

Seems clear we do want to include emails sent to IETF lists, but what about:

- IM chat messages
- slides presented at f2f or online meetings
- I-D and RFC text

We should decide which of the above are in/out of scope for this draft, make that clear and consider any changes/additions flowing from that.

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body: I guess since we're here, we should add issue/PR discussion on github and the like as another possible type of text to consider as in/out of scope:-)

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body: We seem to agree to exclude I-D and RFC text - I'll make a PR for that

comments.author: lllyfeng
comments.body: I think this issue should be closed.:)

issues.title: What kinds of "tell" do we want to note?
issues.author: sftcd
issues.body:
Raised in discussion of #1 

What (additional) kinds of "tell" do we want to describe?

Do we want to include real examples from IETF lists or not?

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body: WRT whether or not to include real examples in the draft, I suspect it'd be better to invent synthetic examples, so as not to annoy people or de-rail subsequent discussion (from talking about our I-D to whatever is pointed-at). We'd also risk pointing at something and having the relevant author deny using AI-tools I guess:-)

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body:
The comment on #1 that triggered this issue was:

> Worth adding one more "tell" alongside the current list (overly positive, geometric terms, phrasing patterns, lack of uncertainty, walls of text): AI output also tends toward an artificially "balanced" stance — hedging between positions instead of committing to one. Slightly different axis from "lack of uncertainty" as currently written (that's about overconfidence in interpreting what others meant) — this one is about under-committing when stating your own position.

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body:
As noted by @lllyfeng in #1:

>On the "balanced stance" tell: yes, it's real. My first post to the DAWN list had the argument but not the attitude — too flat to show where I actually stood. I asked Odyssey to revise it with an explicit instruction to take a clear stance and not worry about offending people. The tone changed noticeably.

> The tell is correctable through prompting, but only if the author notices it first. Worth adding to the workflow section: reviewing AI output for fidelity includes checking whether the LLM's default tendency toward safe, balanced, non-committal prose has diluted what you actually meant to say.

issues.title: Emphasise "IETF should develop guidance" recommendation
issues.author: sftcd
issues.body:
Raised in discussion of #1 

The main, and probably only concrete, recommendation we have is that the IETF should develop guidance.

We should emphasise that, probably by adding it to the abstract/intro.

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body: I think this is fairly easy to handle - we should do it. Happy to make a PR that adds such text to abstract/intro.

comments.author: lllyfeng
comments.body: We all agree with it, so I think this issue can be closed.

issues.title: Should we recommend AI tool users try make their messages more like human messages?
issues.author: sftcd
issues.body:
Raised in discussion on #1 

> Also consider adding: authors should use AI tools/prompting aimed at natural, concise output rather than settling for the default verbose/over-hedged "AI voice." Needs to be paired explicitly with "and still disclose" though — otherwise it reads as tension with "always be transparent" and risk #3 ("reader inability to distinguish"). The point is better writing, not fewer visible tells, so that should be said outright rather than left implicit.

Not clear that the two authors here have the same opinion of that:-)

We should thrash it out.

comments.author: sftcd
comments.body: I need to ponder this one for a bit before deciding what I think about it.

pulls.title: first set of SF suggestions
pulls.author: sftcd
pulls.body:
Here's my initial suggested additions, with some structure change and changes to intro/recommendations. 

Let's discuss!

comments.author: lllyfeng
comments.body:
> Here's my initial suggested additions, with some structure change and changes to intro/recommendations.
> 
> Let's discuss!

stephen，
 I have some comments as below:

Title/scope: narrowing it was the right instinct — the old title ("Human-AI Collaboration in Technical Communities, Principles and Practice") was too broad to say anything concrete. But "Dealing with LLMs in Email Discussions" swings too far the other way — most of the Odyssey workflow section isn't about email at all, it's about drafting documents. I'd rather keep the scope at IETF document writing (I-Ds, slides, etc.) and list discussion, not just the latter. Something like "Dealing with LLMs in IETF Contributions: Documents and List Discussions" keeps it concrete without dropping the document side. Also worth flagging: drafts/slides are one-shot artifacts people can review at leisure, list mail is back-and-forth in near-real-time — the "can a reader trust/tell" argument probably plays out differently in each case, so we may need to treat them separately rather than one blanket claim.

Tone: fully on board with the shift from argumentative to exploratory/tentative — that's the right call, let's keep going that direction rather than walking it back.

A Reader's Concerns: Worth adding one more "tell" alongside the current list (overly positive, geometric terms, phrasing patterns, lack of uncertainty, walls of text): AI output also tends toward an artificially "balanced" stance — hedging between positions instead of committing to one. Slightly different axis from "lack of uncertainty" as currently written (that's about overconfidence in interpreting what others meant) — this one is about under-committing when stating your own position.

Recommendations: Strong agreement on the closing point — IETF should develop guidelines for AI/LLM tooling use in IETF discussions (drafts, slides, list mail). Would make this more prominent rather than tacked on after the bullet list, since it's arguably the most concrete recommendation in the whole draft.

Also consider adding: authors should use AI tools/prompting aimed at natural, concise output rather than settling for the default verbose/over-hedged "AI voice." Needs to be paired explicitly with "and still disclose" though — otherwise it reads as tension with "always be transparent" and risk #3 ("reader inability to distinguish"). The point is better writing, not fewer visible tells, so that should be said outright rather than left implicit.

As for this PR - I'll make issues for the discussion points above and if that's ok suggest we merge this as-is, then work through those issues. Sound OK?
